Response: We thank the reviewer for this important comment and sincerely
apologize for not adequately acknowledging the pioneering work on paper-based
secondary blood group typing in the previous version. We now explicitly cite the key
contributions from Gil Garnier, Shen Wei and others [1–9], who developed paper-based
ABO/RhD devices, rapid droplet- and laser-incubated assays, and bioactive paper
platforms for secondary blood group phenotyping. Their mechanistic exploration of
agglutination and flow behavior on paper cards has provided valuable guidance and
conceptual inspiration for the design and positioning of our own platform.
These studies have been added and described in the Introduction (Line 62), as
below: Point-of-care (POCT) blood typing has attracted considerable attention, and a
number of paper- and fiber-based platforms have already been reported. Li et al.
developed a paper-based blood typing device that reports the patient's ABO/RhD type
"in writing," demonstrating that simple capillary-driven paper cards can support clear
visual readout outside conventional laboratories [1]. Guan et al. later introduced a
barcode-like paper sensor for smartphone-assisted ABO typing, showing the feasibility
of coupling paper cards with digital imaging for semi-quantitative diagnostics [2]. On
the bioactive paper side, Yeow et al. established a paper-based assay for red blood cell
antigen typing using the indirect antiglobulin test, thereby extending paper platforms to
secondary blood group phenotyping under IAT conditions [3]. Hertaeg et al. reported a
rapid droplet-wicking paper method for ABO blood typing, further simplifying on-
paper handling and reducing assay time [4]. Manderson et al. developed droplet-based
paper assays with laser incubation for blood group antibody screening, and
subsequently showed that laser-assisted paper platforms can accelerate the detection of
red cell alloantibodies in human samples [5-6]. Several other groups have proposed
related POCT-oriented formats. Songjaroen et al. designed a simple, low-cost portable
paper-based ABO blood typing device for point-of-care testing [7]. Chomean et al.
reported a paper-based device combined with image-based high-throughput detection
for phenotyping minor blood groups including C, c, E, e and Mia. Min et al. recently
presented a microfluidic cotton-thread analytical device for rapid and easily identifiable
blood typing [8-9]. Collectively, these studies demonstrate that paper and related porous
substrates can support POCT-compatible blood group testing, including secondary
blood group phenotyping, when used with fresh red blood cell reagents. However,

bm
for at least two years at ambient temperature, (ii) enables ABO reverse grouping and
quantitative IgM titration on a single paper device within minutes, and (iii) remains
compatible with secondary blood group phenotyping. In this context, secondary blood
groups in our study are used primarily as proof-of-concept that RBC @Fluo preserves
bm
a broad antigen repertoire.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Methods for accurate, rapid blood typing and antibody titration at the point of care are constrained by cold-chain dependent red blood cell (RBC) reagents, time-consuming serial dilutions, and subjective visual interpretation. To overcome these limitations, here we develop a method based on bioengineered red-blood cells. We engineer hemoglobin-depleted RBC membranes that preserve ABO surface antigens, label them with fluorescent nanoparticles, and lyophilize them, demonstrating at least 2 years of stability at room-temperature. We capture hemagglutination on a dual-layer paper pad and quantify it by fluorescence in approximately 8 minutes, eliminating the need for serial dilution. We conduct a registered clinical trial (ChiCTR2300078864) and benchmark performance against the gel microcolumn assay. In a clinical cohort (n=641), ABO typing achieves 100% concordance. In antibody-titration samples, quantitative titers agree with the gel microcolumn assay (coincidence 80.75%, κ=0.8623). In summary, we develop a cold-chain-independent, handheld paper-based assay that enables simultaneous ABO grouping and quantitative antibody titration with clinical-grade performance, supporting scalable manufacturing, cross-site standardization, and transfusion decision-making in emergency and resource-limited settings.

---

## Introduction

Since the early 20th century, the discovery of blood types has formed the foundation of homologous transfusion, which aims to prevent fatal hemolytic reactions and ensure blood safety in allogeneic transfusions1–3. Landsteiner’s rule states that in the ABO blood group system, an individual’s serum will always contain antibodies against the antigens that are absent from their own red blood cells, and will not contain antibodies against the antigens that are present on their red blood cells. This principle underpins the dual verification mechanism of conventional ABO blood typing4–6. In forward typing tests, commercial anti-A and anti-B antibodies are used to detect the presence of A or B antigens on RBCs, while reverse typing employs standard A- or B-type RBCs to identify anti-A or anti-B antibodies.

Antibody titration quantifies the concentration of specific antibodies relative to blood type antigens in a blood sample. This test is clinically valuable for several reasons: (1) Type O blood lacks both A and B antigens but contains anti-A and anti-B antibodies, which can lead to hemolytic transfusion reactions if present at high titers7. (2) In hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) and organ transplants, monitoring ABO blood type changes and adjusting transfusion strategies based on real-time antibody titration can prevent adverse outcomes8,9. (3) High-dose intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) can cause hemolysis in recipients with A, B, or AB blood types10. (4) Blood type incompatibility between a mother and her newborn may lead to hemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN)11,12.

Traditional methods for blood typing and antibody titration primarily rely on tube testing and GMA13. Tube testing, though simple, is time-consuming and subject to observer variability. GMA uses gel columns and a centrifuge to assess antibody presence based on RBC sedimentation, offering greater accuracy but requiring complex equipment and skilled operators, making it less suitable for time-sensitive or resource-limited settings, such as emergencies, primary care, or battlefield conditions. Paper-based diagnostics (PADs) have emerged to address portability and speed. Commercial formats include consumer agglutination cards and professional GLIF-type tests, which deliver rapid ABO/Rh results but remain qualitative and restricted to forward typing. Point-of-care (POCT) blood typing has attracted considerable attention, and a number of paper- and fiber-based platforms have already been reported. Li et al. developed a paper-based blood typing device that reports the patient’s ABO/RhD type “in writing,” demonstrating that simple capillary-driven paper cards can support clear visual readout outside conventional laboratories14. Guan et al. later introduced a barcode-like paper sensor for smartphone-assisted ABO typing, showing the feasibility of coupling paper cards with digital imaging for semi-quantitative diagnostics15. On the bioactive paper side, Yeow et al. established a paper-based assay for red blood cell antigen typing using the indirect antiglobulin test, thereby extending paper platforms to secondary blood group phenotyping under IAT conditions16. Hertaeg et al. reported a rapid droplet-wicking paper method for ABO blood typing, further simplifying on-paper handling and reducing assay time17. Manderson et al. developed droplet-based paper assays with laser incubation for blood group antibody screening, and subsequently showed that laser-assisted paper platforms can accelerate the detection of red cell alloantibodies in human samples18,19. Several other groups have proposed related POCT-oriented formats. Songjaroen et al. designed a simple, low-cost portable paper-based ABO blood typing device for point-of-care testing20. Chomean et al. reported a paper-based device combined with image-based high-throughput detection for phenotyping minor blood groups, including C, c, E, e, and Mia21. Min et al. recently presented a microfluidic cotton-thread analytical device for rapid and easily identifiable blood typing22. Collectively, these studies demonstrate that paper and related porous substrates can support POCT-compatible blood group testing, including secondary blood group phenotyping, when used with fresh red blood cell reagents. However, existing platforms generally rely on short-lived cell reagents with limited ambient stability and are not designed to provide long-term preserved red cell reagents that simultaneously support rapid ABO reverse grouping and quantitative IgM antibody titration.

Several research teams have attempted to develop freezing methods for rare blood type RBCs23,24. However, progress has been limited due to the challenge of preventing ice crystal formation in the cytoplasm during freezing, which causes RBC membrane rupture during rehydration. Furthermore, prolonged freezing increases the likelihood of ice nucleation, which can alter the structure of membrane proteins structures, reducing their ability to bind to antibodies25,26. Thus, preserving the antigenicity of RBCs for antibody testing remains a significant challenge.

Antibody titration typically involves serial dilution of serum, followed by mixing each dilution with antigen-positive RBCs to determine the highest dilution at which agglutination occurs4. Despite its use, this method has limitations: (1) Sensitivity and precision, especially when the antibody concentration falls between two dilution points; (2) Resource and time consumption; (3) Cumulative dilution errors.

To address these limitations, we propose a rapid method for detecting IgM anti-A and anti-B antibodies using bioengineered RBCs and fluorescent labeling. The key innovation lies in the modification and freeze-drying of RBCs to create long-lasting RBC membranes that preserve functional antigens. RBCs are converted into RBC membranes using a gentle punching solution, which removes cellular components like hemoglobin while preserving the antigenicity. This process, combined with freeze-drying, allows long-term storage at room temperature. Fluorescent nano-labeling technology enables agglutination to be visualized and analyzed quantitatively using a fluorescence analyzer, eliminating the subjectivity of visual interpretation. We developed a paper-based fluorescent assay (PFA) based on agglutination principles, in which antibody level correlates with the size and number of agglutinated clumps. Blood typing and antibody titration are completed simultaneously in less than 8 min, meeting point-of-care testing needs.

Following establishment of this method, we conducted a clinical trial (ChiCTR2300078864) to assess assay performance. The RBC bioengineering approach is extensible to the storage of rare blood type antigens and is adaptable for membrane protein preservation. These innovations reduce operational complexity and equipment dependency, providing a solution for rapid testing in specialized environments. More importantly, the fluorescent labeling system enables precise quantification, presenting a potential breakthrough for IgG/IgM antibody quantitative detection techniques.

---

## Results

PFA design for BG-Ab testing
Our research focuses on developing a POCT assay for BG-Ab analysis (Fig. 1). Traditional BG-Ab testing relies heavily on fresh RBC reagents, requiring cold chain storage. These reagents induce agglutination of RBCs by specific BG-Ab. Major blood group antigens such as ABO, Rh, Kell, and Duffy are inherent components of the RBC membrane, rather than being adsorbed from plasma onto the RBC surface (e.g., Lewis system)27, and storage-related damage can compromise antigenicity28. RBCs consist of a cell membrane and contents such as hemoglobin and enzymes, but lack nuclei and organelles29, we hypothesized that removing the RBC contents while maintaining the membrane structure would extend the storage life of RBC reagents. To test this, we use a mild punching solution to release RBC contents and prepare RBC biomembranes (RBCbm), preserving the antigenicity of the RBC membrane surface.

Since removing hemoglobin eliminates color indication on RBCs, we label the RBCbm with red FNPs using click chemistry, creating nano-markers to visualize and monitor agglutination. The resulting RBCbm labeled with FNPs is referred to as RBCbm@Fluo. The design allows for the separation of RBC-based clots from free ones, making it possible to directly read the agglutination extent via fluorescent signals. Thus eliminating subjective interpretation and bypasseing the lengthy dilution process (Fig. 1a). Furthermore, freeze-drying enhances the practicality of RBCbm@Fluo. After freeze-drying, the reagent can be stored at room temperature for extended periods, making it ideal for emergency settings, such as ambulances, field environments, aircraft, and ships. It is also suitable for laboratory use. As shown in Fig. 1b, RBCbm@Fluo works based blood agglutination principles. When a test sample containing BG-Ab is added, an antigen-antibody reaction occurs, resulting in visible aggregates or precipitates. The size and number of aggregates correlate with antibody concentration.

To facilitate on-site BG-Ab testing, we developed a paper-based fluorescent assay (PFA) that integrates the RBCbm@Fluo (Fig. 1c). The device, constructed using 3D printing, offers significant advantages for producing cost-effective prototypes. RBCbm@Fluo is freeze-dried onto the reaction zone’s wells, and unaggregated RBCbm@Fluo is removed via on-site filtration before result reading. The filtration membrane consists of two layers: an upper pre-filter that retain larger aggregates, while the lower fine filter membrane that captures smaller aggregates. Additionally, a location well is included for sample positioning and calibration, aiding auto-focusing and image correction. As a result, the concentration of blood group antibodies can be precisely quantified using a portable fluorescence analyzer.

The current focus of the PFA platform is on detecting IgM anti-A and anti-B antibodies (Fig. 1d). Additionally, the platform can be adapted to detect IgG antibodies by adding anti-human globulin (AHG) reagents and incubating at 37 °C. This expanded application is particularly useful for diagnosing hemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN), irregular antibody screening, and direct/indirect Coombs’ tests, thereby providing a broader diagnostic toolset for clinical applications. In future developments, we plan to enhance the PFA’s performance by integrating automation. We aim to integrate a rotating disk with an automated manipulator, which will increase sample processing capacity and improve detection efficiency (Fig. 1e). For instance, a single disk could accommodate 32 samples, enabling up to 240 results per hour—more than a 30-fold increase in efficiency.

Preparation and evaluation of RBCbm@Fluo
Conventionally, RBC bio-membrane processing and extraction methods rely on hypotonic lysis and repetitive freeze-thaw cycles. However, these methods often cause varying degrees of membrane fragmentation, which can damage surface antigens and reduce antigenicity. To address this issue, we have developed an optimized mild method. This approach uses an extremely low concentration of cell-punching reagents (e.g., Triton) to release intracellular components such as hemoglobin while preserving the integrity of the RBC membrane and avoiding antigenicity loss caused by membrane fragmentation. Our experimental results demonstrate that RBC bio-membranes prepared using this mild method exhibit significantly higher agglutination scores (59.60±0.89) when observed under a fluorescent flashlight, compared to the hypotonic lysis method (49.80±1.83) and the repeated freeze-thaw method (41.20±1.64) (Supplementary Table 1). Detailed scoring for different titers is provided in Supplementary Table 2, based on AABB guidelines30–32. Imaging flow cytometry analysis confirmed that RBCbm prepared using the mild punching method maintains a clear and uniform cell-like morphology, similar to that of the original RBCs (Supplementary Fig. 1), demonstrating the superiority of this method in preserving RBC bio-membrane integrity.

The color of RBCs, derived from hemoglobin, is often used as an indicator in clinical tests involving RBC reagents. After hemoglobin release, we introduced FNPs instead of commercially available gold nanoparticles or latex beads to modify the RBC bio-membrane as nano-markers (Fig. 2a). This was aimed to achieving high sensitivity and accurate quantification. We selected 200 nm-sized spherical red FNPs, with carboxyl groups on their surfaces. These FNPs exhibited excellent fluorescence stability with an excitation wavelength of 365 nm and an emission wavelength of 610 nm, ensuring minimal interference from ambient visible light (Supplementary Fig. 2a). Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis revealed a uniformly ordered arrangement of FNPs (Supplementary Fig. 2b). A simple and rapid click reaction formed stable peptide bonds between the RBCbm and FNPs, preserving the physiological and chemical properties of the RBC membrane.

To optimize fluorescence intensity and signal-to-noise ratio, labeling conditions were adjusted (Supplementary Fig. 3). TEM images for RBCbm@Fluo (Fig. 1a) demonstrated that the membrane structure was preserved, with FNPs uniformly distributed on the outer surface, supporting the feasibility of our bioengineering strategy. Supplementary Fig. 5 shows that, when excited by a UV fluorescent flashlight, the particles emit bright red fluorescence, which is also visible to the naked eye at high concentrations (Supplementary Fig. 4).

We conducted a comparative analysis of the morphological characteristics of RBCs, RBCbm, and RBCbm@Fluo using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (Fig. 2b). RBCs exhibited their typical biconcave disc shape, while RBCbm resembled deflated balloons, with cellular contents released but the membrane structure preserved. Due to the stretching effect of the FNPs, the RBCbm adopted various shapes and sizes. (Supplementary Fig. 5). Atomic force microscopy (AFM) results supported these observations (Supplementary Fig. 6). The phospholipid bilayer provides structural support for the membrane, maintaining cellular stability and integrity. Confocal microscopy analyses confirmed that RBCbm@Fluo preparation introduced visible alterations in the phospholipid bilayer (Supplementary Fig. 7a), membrane proteins (e.g., CD47) (Supplementary Fig. 7b), and cytoskeletal elements such as microtubules and microfilaments (Fig. 2c). Although there was mild structural disruption in the cytoskeleton, the overall cell morphology remained intact.

Dynamic light scattering (DLS) measurements showed that the hydrodynamic diameter for RBCbm and RBCbm@Fluo were 7.04±0.37 μm, 3.40±0.18 μm, and 4.00±0.08 μm, respectively. The slight increase in size for RBCbm@Fluo can be attributed to the attachment of FNPs (Fig. 2d). Zeta potential measurements revealed values of −30.43±1.14 mV for RBCs, −50.63±5.30 mV for RBCbm, and −47.60±5.17 mV for RBCbm@Fluo (Fig. 2e). Flow cytometry analysis indicated that the average recoveries were 93.78±1.24% for RBCbm and 85.23±2.15% for RBCbm@Fluo to the origin RBC (Fig. 2f), indicating the feasibility of large-scale preparation and future applications.

In summary, since our bioengineering approach induces certain changes in the shape, mechanical properties, and size of the RBCs, we successfully developed a RBC bio-membrane-based substitute for standard RBC reagents, providing a reliable, sensitive, and robust platform for blood type antibody detection and other diagnostic applications.

Next, we evaluated the performance of RBCbm@Fluo by examining several key aspects, including antigenicity, specificity, antigen strength, and affinity. Commercial standard human RBC reverse typing reagents were used as the starting reagents for RBCbm@Fluo preparation and served as positive controls. The agglutination induced by the blood type antigen-antibody reaction was similar between RBCs and RBCbm@Fluo (Fig. 2g–i), with the total agglutination score matching closely between the two (Fig. 2j). Detailed scores at different titers are provided in Supplementary Table 3. Notably, the agglutination status was easier to distinguish with RBCbm@Fluo when excited by a fluorescent flashlight and observed with the naked eye. The degree of agglutination varied with different antibody titers, as observed both visually (Fig. 2h) and through fluorescence imaging (Fig. 2i). These results indicate that the antigenicity and specificity of RBCbm@Fluo are at least comparable to those of the RBC reagent. The antigenicity, antigen strength, and specificity of RBCbm@Fluo also comply with the “Technical Review Guidelines for Registration of Human Red Blood Cell Reverse Typing Reagents” issued by the National Medical Products Administration of China, as shown in Supplementary Tables 4–6.

Flow cytometry analysis revealed a reduction in the expression levels of CD47 and blood group A antigen to approximately 60% and 51%, respectively (Fig. 2k, l). We attribute this reduction to two factors: the pore-forming process during RBCbm@Fluo preparation and the labeling of FNPs, which may have led to partial shielding of the surface antigens. Bio-Layer Interferometry (BLI) was used to measure the affinity index (Kd) for antigen-antibody reactions (Fig. 2m and Supplementary Fig. 9). Although significant reduction between RBCbm@Fluo (2.31×10-8) and RBCbm (7.00×10-8) was observed, the fact that they are of the same order of magnitude might indicate that FNPs labeling resulted in a slight injury to the binding affinity. Despite the minor unavoidable damage, the results in Fig. 2 confirm that RBCbm@Fluo retains the necessary characteristics for effective use in reverse typing and antibody titration determination.

To ensure batch-to-batch consistency, imaging flow cytometry was employed to assess RBCbm@Fluo count, membrane surface antigen expression levels, and degree of aggregation as part of quality control, with the coefficient of variation regulated to remain below 15%.

In addition, we validated the feasibility of RBCbm@Fluo for detecting antibodies beyond ABO by testing secondary blood group systems and IgG-class antibodies. We assembled a panel covering Rh (D, C, E, c, e), Kell (K), Duffy (Fya, Fyb), Lewis (Lea, Leb), and MNS (M, N), using commercially available irregular-antibody screening RBC reagents as source materials to prepare RBCbm@Fluo. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 10A, RBCbm@Fluo exhibited the expected antigen profiles. In Supplementary Fig. 10B, agglutination patterns and intensities for the IgG panels (Rh, Kell, Duffy) and the IgM panels (Lewis, MNS) closely matched those of standard commercial reagents, indicating preservation of the relevant antigenic determinants and effective recapitulation of reactivity across multiple systems. Collectively, these results support the feasibility of RBCbm@Fluo for detecting IgG antibodies and secondary blood group systems.

Freeze-dried preservation of RBCbm@Fluo
To further expand the practicality of RBCbm@Fluo, freeze-drying was considered for the long-term ambient storage instead of the typical liquid state used for commercial reagent RBCs (Fig. 3a, b). The mass of RBCbm was measured to be c.a. 44% of the normal RBCs (Fig. 3c), namely, the majority of the H2O might have been removed along with the hemoglobin. This greatly reduced formation of intracellular ice crystals and the membrane rupture during rehydration. A detailed freeze-drying procedure was provided in Supplementary Fig. 11 and Supplementary Table 7. After freeze-drying, RBCbm@Fluo appeared as white, uniform, loose, and power-like substance with an average moisture content reducing to (4.37±0.32)%, meeting the requirements for effective freeze-drying (Fig. 3b). When rehydration by gently shaking in sterile water, it rapidly dissolved into a clear liquid without unexpected aggregation and showed uniform fluorescence under UV light. The microscopic morphology of RBCbm@Fluo after freeze-drying and rehydration is shown in Fig. 3d, e. No noticeable detachment of the fluorescent beads, indicating that the freeze-drying process did not harm the FNPs.

Next, we evaluated the functionality of RBCbm@Fluo post freeze-drying. Nano-flow cytometry revealed that freeze dry did not significant damage to membrane protein expression of CD47 and blood group A antigen (Fig. 3f, g). Agglutination performance of rehydrated RBCbm@Fluo was also assessed, showing no significant differences compared to the original (Fig. 3h). Figure 3i shows that the fluorescence intensity of freeze-dried RBCbm@Fluo remained stable when stored at RT for 1 year, with a decrease of no more than 5% could by the end of the second year.

We further calculated the agglutination scores of RBCbm@Fluo (Fig. 3j and Supplementary Table 8). Results showed the liquid RBC reagent stored at 4 °C became unusable after three months due to severe hemolysis. If RBCbm@Fluo were stored as a liquid at 4 °C, it would experience a c.a. 20% decrease in agglutination scores within three months, agreeing with the quality guarantee period for commercial RBC reagents. Further, it showed a c.a. 70% decrease 6 months later, corresponding to the complete loss of function in agglutination. In contrast, the freeze-dried RBCbm@Fluo maintained stable detection performance throughout a 2-year storage period (Fig. 3j), with less than 10% in agglutination score. In summary, freeze-drying extends the shelf life of RBCbm@Fluo to 2 years, preserving antigenicity and agglutination performance, making it a reliable substitute for commercial RBC reagents.

Establishment of BG-Ab analysis method
We developed a paper-based POCT device for on-site BG-Ab analysis with high accuracy. To optimize the device’s design, we explored three design: baffle type, push-pull type, and flip type (Supplementary Figs. 12 and 13). The flip-type was selected as the optimal choice to minimize operational errors. The device consists of two distinct zones: a foldable reaction zone and a filtration zone (Fig. 4a). The front view (Fig. 4b) shows three reaction wells in the reaction zone and corresponding filtration wells below in the filtration zone. Freeze-dried RBCbm@Fluo is uniformly distributed at the bottom of the reaction wells, where rehydration occurs, and BG-Ab-induced agglutination takes place.

Once the agglutination process is complete, the operator folds the reaction zone, allowing the mixture to flow into the filtration zone under gravity. To eliminate background signals from unaggregated free RBCbm@Fluo, the filtration zone consists of four layers, a filtration membrane, a super-hydrophilic pad, an elastic glass fiber pad, an absorbent pad (Fig. 4c). The first layer separates blood clots from unagglutinated RBCbm@Fluo, while the second layer accelerates filtration. The third layer provides lateral capillary action, and the fourth layer captures the filtrate.

We tested nylon membranes with pore sizes ranging from 1 to 100 μm for refined filtration, selecting a 1–2 μm-sized membrane that effectively captured all visible aggregates based on SEM results (Supplementary Fig. 14). However, a single layer led to clogging due to larger aggregates, so we incorporated a 5 μm pore-size glass fiber pre-filter to trap larger aggregates (Fig. 4d, e). This multi-layer design efficiently separates aggregates relevant for analysis, enhancing sensitivity and precision of fluorescence detection.

The operational process of the PFA is shown in Fig. 4f. First, 60 μL of plasma is added to the reaction zone, followed by gentle shaking to ensure thorough mixing. After five minutes, the operator flips the bottom cover, allowing the liquid to flow into the filtration zone. The liquid passes through both the pre-filter and fine particle filter, retaining aggregates while removing unaggregated RBCbm@Fluo. As shown in Fig. 4g, the fluorescence intensity of the aggregates likely correlates with the antibody concentration, and a fluorescence analyzer measures the total intensity to indicate both the blood group and antibody titer.

We further validated the separation performance of the pre-filter and fine particle filter through confocal microscopy (Fig. 4h). Standard BG-Ab samples diluted in serial dilutions were analyzed using the PFA. The results confirmed that the pre-filter primarily captured larger aggregates, while the fine particle filter trapped smaller ones. This dual-layer filtration design effectively separates aggregates from non-aggregated RBCbm@Fluo, enhancing BG-Ab detection accuracy.

Next, we optimized key parameters, such as dilution factor, RBCbm@Fluo concentration, sample volume, reaction time, and washing buffer volume. Supplementary Fig. 15 gave the direct fluorescence readout using the standard reagent. Taking the titer distribution of the population worldwide into consideration33–36, the dilution factor of 8 was identified to ensure that the linear range would locate in the most needed region, even if there was some loss in sensitivity. Then we used the slope of the linear regression equation to evaluate the optimal parameters, with a higher slope indicating a stronger dependence of fluorescence intensity on the special amounts of antibodies. The variable of sample volume was optimized completely accordingly. And 60 μL was selected out (Fig. 5b). For the dosage of RBCbm@Fluo (Fig. 5a), it was obvious that 200 mg/L gave the higher slope than 100 mg/L, but 100 mg/L was selected for its linear correlation and cost-effectiveness. So was the choice for the volume of washing buffer 150 μL (Fig. 5d). As to the reaction time, 5 min and 10 min gave nearly identical results, so 5 min was selected for efficiency (Fig. 5c).

We tested the PFA’s performance by differentiating standard substance with IgM anti-A antibody ranging from 1:16 to 1:512, yielding a strong linear regression (r2=0.98) (Fig. 5e). Fluorescence intensity correlated with antibody titer within this range, and UV light images provides intuitive evidence (Fig. 5f). So was the case for IgM anti-B antibody (Supplementary Fig. 16). Confocal microscopy images of the agglutinates on the filtration membrane showed that as the titer increased, both the quantity and density of agglutinates increased (Fig. 5g), supporting the superior performance of the PFA within the linear.

We further tested the robustness of the PFA by simulating common interference factors: hemolysis, lipemia, and jaundice. Samples with hemolysis rates of 0.08% (non-hemolytic), 0.8% (hemolytic), and 8% (highly hemolytic). The results showed that hemolysis up to 8% had no significant impact on detection (Fig. 5h). We also simulated lipemia and jaundice by adding cholesterol and bilirubin to the plasma. While lipemia at levels ≥9 mmol/L weakened agglutination (Supplementary Fig. 17), normal cholesterol levels (below 6 mmol/L) did not affect results (Fig. 5i). Of course, such phenomenon also occurs in commercially available RBC reagents. Bilirubin levels below 600 had no significant effect on the test results (Fig. 5j), demonstrating the PFA’s resilience to common clinical interferences.

Clinical evaluation of the PFA assay
We obtained clinical plasma samples from a hospital and employed the as-prepared PFA for blood typing and antibody titer determination. Geographic distributions of the subjects are detailed in Supplementary Fig. 18. Routine blood typing methods used in the hospital include the tube method and the gel microcolumn agglutination (GMA). While the tube method is considered a clinical gold standard, its accuracy and consistency can be influenced by manual operation and subjective interpretation. In contrast, GMA is highly automated, with standardized the gel microcolumn cards, minimizing operational errors and improving reproducibility. To compare the PFA with GMA, a double-blind clinical trial was conducted, registered as ChiCTR2300078864. Our present clinical data mainly reflect Chinese Han donors from Fujian and do not systematically cover rare antigen variants.

Figure 6a presents the representative blood group reverse typing results for Types A, B, AB, and O using the PFA, while Fig. 6b displays images under UV fluorescent light. Threshold values for positive and negative results were established using 216 clinical samples previously determined by the GMA. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve and area under the curve (AUC) analysis determined optimal cutoff values: 998 a.u. for IgM anti-A antibodies and 987 a.u. for IgM anti-B antibodies (Fig. 6c). At these thresholds, specificity and sensitivity reached 100% (Fig. 6d).

Next, 641 clinical plasma samples with unknown blood types were tested, recording fluorescence intensity values. Results revealed 188 Type A, 143 Type B, 48 Type AB, and 262 Type O, yielding a concordance rate of 100% (Fig. 6e and Supplementary Tables 9 and 10). These findings demonstrate that the PFA exhibits excellent accuracy in blood group typing.

To determine thresholds for antibody titer detection, 245 samples were tested to cover each titer interval with a target of at least 50 per interval, confirmed by GMA. These samples were tested using the PFA, and the corresponding fluorescence intensity values were recorded (Supplementary Fig. 19a, d). ROC and AUC analysis yielded cutoff values for IgM anti-A antibodies: 636 a.u. (1:16), 1193 a.u. (1:32), 2757 a.u. (1:64), 4337 a.u. (1:128), and 4896 a.u. (1:256) (Fig. 6f). Similarly, for IgM anti-B antibodies, 599 a.u. (1:16), 1175 a.u. (1:32), 2777 a.u. (1:64), 4467 a.u. (1:128), and 4916 a.u. (1:256) (Fig. 6g).

We then measured antibody titers of 388 clinical samples using both the PFA and GMA in parallel. Fluorescence intensity distributions for total IgM anti-A and anti-B titers are presented in Fig. 6h, i (left), respectively. Minimal overlap between adjacent titer levels highlights the PFA’s precision. The Pearson correlation coefficients between the PFA and GMA were r²=0.8813, r=0.939 (anti-A) and r²=0.8788, r=0.937 (anti-B), indicating strong positive correlations (Fig. 6h, i right).

As shown in Table 1, the PFA demonstrated strong reliability and accuracy, with an overall coincidence rate of 80.75%, Cohen’s Kappa of 0.8623, and a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.8853. And 100% were within ±1 twofold-dilution step. For anti-A and anti-B titers, coincidence rates were 81.03% and 80.47%, Cohen’s Kappa values were 0.8642 and 0.8601, and Pearson correlation coefficients were 0.8726 and 0.9029, respectively. Concordance rates for different blood types were similarly high: type A (anti-B), 81.37%, type B (anti-A) 74.29%, type O (anti-A) 84.77%, type O (anti-B) 80.79% (Fig. 6j–m and Table 1). At the clinically relevant cutoff of 1:128 (low- vs high-titer), the 2×2 confusion matrix (TP=26, FN=4, FP=12, TN=467) yields a PPA of 86.7% (26/30) and an NPA of 97.5% (467/479) between PFA and GMA (Supplementary Fig. 20).

Concordance differences were largely due to the absence of a fully quantitative clinical reference. Antibody titers were compared against the semi-quantitative GMA, whose discrete dilution endpoints introduce subjectivity near cut-offs. In our dataset, 19.25% of samples at the clinical decision threshold were discordant; 85% of these fell within “threshold ±10%,” consistent with borderline calls inherent to semi-quantitative reads rather than PFA error. Methodological behavior also differed across titer ranges: the PFA detected weak, low-titer agglutination that can be under-recognized by GMA, whereas high-titer endpoints were occasionally assigned one dilution step apart—within the 1–2 step variability reported for traditional titrations. Overall, the PFA achieved high ABO typing accuracy and yielded quantitative, fluorescence-based titers with satisfactory agreement to GMA, reducing subjective interpretation around borderline results.

## Methods

Ethical statement
The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of The 909th Hospital (Southeast Hospital of Xiamen University), School of Medicine, Xiamen University (Ethical approval number: L2023002), where all clinical samples were collected. Written informed consent was waived because only leftover clinical specimens were used with no additional risk, and all data were handled under a double-blinded design to protect privacy; the study was approved by the Institutional Review Board in accordance with in vitro diagnostic reagent clinical trial technical guidelines. Written consent for publication was not required.

Preparation of RBCbm
RBC suspensions were obtained from Changchun Bioxun Biotechnology Co., Ltd. The blood was sourced from healthy adult donors who underwent screening for five markers in compliance with national regulations, including transaminase, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, syphilis, and HIV. A1 cells contained both A and A1 antigens, B cells contained B antigens, and O cells contained neither A nor B antigens. The RBC suspension was centrifuged at 1000×g for 10 min to separate the packed red blood cells from the preservative solution. The supernatant was discarded, leaving behind the packed RBCs, which were then subjected to extensive washing and lysis steps to isolate the RBCbm. The RBCbm were prepared using the following three methods: (1) Hypotonic lysis method: 1 mL of RBC precipitate was suspended in 10 mL of 0.25× PBS (Wuhan Servicebio Technology Co., Ltd), causing the cells to swell and rupture, releasing hemoglobin and leaving behind the RBC membrane. The suspension was then washed 3–5 times with an equal volume of distilled water to separate the RBCbm. (2) Repeated freeze-thaw method: 1 mL of RBC precipitate was frozen at −30 °C and then rapidly thawed. This freeze-thaw cycle was repeated 3–5 times, after which the ruptured RBCs were centrifuged. The RBCbm were then washed 3–5 times with 1 mL of distilled water. (3) Mild punching method: 1 mL of RBC precipitate was mixed with 1 mL of punching solution. The mixture was centrifuged to rupture the RBCs, and the RBCbm were separated by washing 3 times with 1 mL of distilled water.

Preparation of RBCbm@Fluo
Take 10 μL of fluorescent nanoparticles (FNPs, MF02, Madenew Biotechnology, China) (solid content: 5.03%, 200 nm, red fluorescence) and disperse them in ultrapure water. Add 200 μL of freshly prepared 1-ethyl-3-(3-dimethylaminopropyl) carbodiimide (EDC, 22981, Thermo Fisher Scientific, US) solution (15 mg/mL) to the dispersion, and sonicate for 1 min to ensure uniform particle dispersion. Incubate the solution at room temperature for 30 min to fully activate the carboxyl groups on the nanoparticle surface. After activation, add 200 μg of RBCbm, prepared using the mild punching method with gentle lysis buffer. Wash with 1 mL of ultrapure water and centrifuge at 6000×g for 5 min to remove unbound materials. Finally, resuspend the engineered RBC bio-membrane (RBCbm@Fluo) in Alsever’s solution (R1016, Solarbio, Beijing, China) and store at 4 °C for future use.

Antigenicity and specificity
Taking A-type RBCs as an example, 50 μL of RBC/RBCbm@Fluo is mixed with 50 μL of IgM anti-A, anti-A1, anti-B, anti-AB, and anti-H antibodies (National Institutes of Food and Drug Control, China). The agglutination strength is then observed and recorded.

Agglutination score
Taking A-type RBCs as an example, IgM anti-A antibodies are serially diluted in a 2-fold series with dilution factors of 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, and 64. For each dilution, 50 μL of the solution is mixed with 50 μL of RBC/RBCbm@Fluo, and agglutination is visually observed at each dilution level. Based on the agglutination strength, a score is assigned following the AABB guidelines 22-24. The agglutination score for each dilution is numerically quantified according to the intensity of the reaction. The scores for all dilutions are then summed to obtain the total agglutination score.

FACS analysis
1×106 cells were harvested by centrifugation at 3000×g for 5 min and then stained with the corresponding antibodies for 20 minutes. The reaction was stopped by washing the cells twice with PBS, and the cells were subsequently analyzed using FACS (BD Biosciences, US). Data were collected and analyzed with FlowJo V10 software.

Characterization of RBCbm@Fluo
The morphology of RBC, RBCbm, and RBCbm@Fluo was observed using Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM, Bruker Dimension ICON, Germany), Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM, Hitachi H-7800, Japan), and Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM, Hitachi SU8220, Japan). RBC, RBCbm, and RBCbm@Fluo were stained with DIL dye (Uelandy, D4053) and CD47 (BD Bioscience, 568090), respectively, and images were recorded using a Laser Scanning Confocal Microscope (Zeiss LSM900, Germany). The hydrodynamic size and Zeta potential of RBC, RBCbm, and RBCbm@Fluo were measured using the Zetasizer Nano ZS90 system. The excitation and emission spectra of nanoparticles were characterized using a Steady-State and Transient Fluorescence Spectrometer (FLS980, Shimadzu, Japan), with fluorescence spectra recorded in the range of 200–800 nm. The number of RBC, RBCbm, and RBCbm@Fluo cells in 10 μL samples was counted using flow cytometry (BD Biosciences), and recovery was calculated accordingly.

Cytoskeleton of RBCbm@Fluo
After collecting the RBC, RBCbm, and RBCbm@Fluo samples, 1 mL of 4% paraformaldehyde (Solarbio, P1110) was added, and the samples were fixed at room temperature for 15 min, followed by three washes. Purified mouse anti-β-Tubulin (Abcam, 556321) was then added, and the samples were incubated overnight, with three washes repeated during the incubation. On the following day, FITC Goat Anti-Mouse Ig (Abcam, 554001) and Phalloidin-iFluor 594 (Abcam, 176757) were added, and the samples were incubated at room temperature for 1 h, followed by another three washes. Next, 500 μL of the samples were plated into confocal microscope wells at a density of 1×106 cells per well and incubated at room temperature in the dark for 30 min to allow the cells to settle at the bottom. Finally, cell morphology and cytoskeletal analysis were performed using a confocal laser scanning microscope (Zeiss LSM900, Germany).

Nanoflow cytometry
The expression of CD47 (PE Mouse Anti-Human CD47, BD Bioscience, 568090) and Blood Group A (PE Blood Group A, Abcam, 565385) on RBCbm@Fluo was detected using the Flow NanoAnalyzer (U30E, NanoFCM).

Bio-layer interferometry
The interaction between blood group antigens and antibodies was analyzed using Bio-Layer Interferometry (BLI, GatorPrime, China). The arrangement and procedures for the samples and probes are outlined in Supplementary Fig. 8. A Max plate was prepared, with 250 μL of PBS added to each well, totaling 24 wells arranged in three rows, with one sensor per well. Bio-WGA was diluted to 20 μg/mL. RBC, RBCbm, and RBCbm@Fluo were diluted to a concentration of 1×108 cells/mL. IgM was serially diluted from 1000 μg/mL in a two-fold gradient, resulting in seven different concentrations. After the reaction was completed, data analysis was performed using the built-in Gator software, and the results were extracted.

Observation of RBCbm@Fluo agglutination on paper
RBCbm@Fluo was previously labeled with DiI (Uelandy, D4053). Following agglutination, the pre-filter and fine particle filter of the nitrocellulose membrane were removed, cut into 5.98 mm × 5.98 mm pieces, and air-dried at room temperature for 48 hours. The samples were then placed onto glass slides for confocal imaging. Microscopic images were captured from the side where the sample was introduced. A Zeiss LSM880 Confocal Microscope was used to generate the confocal micrographs, with a 20× dry objective lens employed for imaging. Images of RBCs within the antibody-treated paper were captured as x–y images or as a series of x–y images with stepped variations in the z-direction, which were then used to construct 3D images (or z-stack images). The resolution of all images was 2048×2048 pixels, and the step width for the z-stack images was 100 μm.

Performance evaluation of RBCbm@Fluo
The formation of RBC agglutinates by RBCbm@Fluo at different antibody titers was analyzed using a confocal microscope (Zeiss LSM880, Germany). First, 1×109 A-type RBCbm@Fluo samples were taken, and DIL dye (Uelandy, D4053) was diluted at a 1:1000 ratio. Then, 5 μL of the diluted dye was added to the samples and incubated in the dark for 15 min. Afterward, the samples were washed three times to obtain DIL-labeled RBCbm@Fluo, which was then resuspended in 1 mL of buffer. Standard IgM anti-A antibody solutions were serially diluted in a 2- to 256-fold range. 100 μL of each dilution of IgM anti-A antibody solution was added to separate wells on the confocal microscope slide, with IgM anti-B antibody used as a negative control. After adding 100 μL of DIL-labeled RBCbm@Fluo to each well, the mixture was gently agitated for 5 min at room temperature to ensure thorough mixing. The reaction was then observed, and images were captured using the confocal microscope.

Secondary blood group and IgG antibody detection
Commercially available irregular antibody screening RBC reagents from Changchun Bioxun Biotechnology Co., Ltd were used as source materials to prepare engineered RBCs. Blood group antibodies covering Rh (D, C, E, c, e), Kell (K), Duffy (Fya, Fyb), Lewis (Lea, Leb), and MNS (M, N) systems were tested, with Rh, Kell, and Duffy as IgG-type antibodies, and Lewis and MNS as IgM-type antibodies. Anti-D (IgG), anti-M, and anti-N antibodies were purchased from the Shanghai Blood Center; human-derived anti-C, anti-E, anti-c, and anti-e (IgG) antibodies were kindly provided by the Guangzhou Blood Center; anti-K, anti-Lea, anti-Leb, and anti-Fya antibodies were obtained from CE-ID, and anti-Fyb antibody from Immunocor. For IgG antibody testing, 20 μL of RBCbm was mixed with 60 μL of the corresponding antibody and 50 μL of anti-human globulin (AHG), incubated at 37 °C for 15 min in a tube, and subsequently transferred to a glass slide for agglutination assessment. For IgM antibodies, 20 μL of RBCbm was mixed with 60 μL of the respective antibody and applied directly to a glass slide for agglutination assessment.

Freeze-dry of RBCbm@Fluo
RBCbm@Fluo was centrifuged to remove Alsever’s solution, and the precipitate was dissolved in freeze-dried protective fluid (FDPF). FDPF, provided by Anbio (Xiamen) Biotechnology Co., Ltd., mainly contains BSA, trehalose, Tris-HCl buffer, and antibiotics. The samples were then subjected to phase-wise freeze-drying in a freeze dryer (LGJ-S40, The Fourth Ring, China) for a total of 26 h. The detailed freeze-drying process is described in Supplementary Fig. 5. After freeze-drying, the appearance of the samples was visually inspected to confirm proper formation. An electronic balance was used to weigh an appropriate amount of the plasma freeze-dried preparation. The moisture content of the freeze-dried preparation was determined using a Karl Fischer moisture meter (Mettler Toledo C30, Switzerland) based on the Coulometric principle. The morphology of the freeze-dried RBCbm@Fluo was observed using Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM, Hitachi SU8220, Japan).

Constructing the paper-based POCT device
(1) Layer-by-layer paper strip assembly in the filtration zone: The paper strip consists of four layers: a filtering membrane, a super-hydrophilic pad (Xinhua 347, China), an elastic glass fiber pad (Boang 1200-015, China), and an absorbent pad (Cobetter, China). The filtering membrane is composed of two components: a pre-filter (Cobetter, China) and a fine particle filter (Munktell MG1502, Sweden). Each material is cut into 29.8 mm wide rectangles using scissors. The materials are then aligned along their edges and bonded at the long edge using a hot glue gun (Deli DL5044, China). Finally, the assembled layers are cut into 29.8 mm × 5.98 mm strips using a CNC high-speed cutter (Jinbiao ZQ3500/ZQ3501, China). (2) Paper-based POCT device: We designed the device for reverse typing and antibody titration using SolidWorks to create a 3D model. The model was then printed with an epoxy resin material using a 3D printer (REMP 3D HD600, China). To prevent interference from the material’s inherent fluorescence, the surface was coated with UV paint to achieve a matte black finish. (3) Fluorescence Analyzer: The matching fluorescence analyzer was designed and manufactured by Anbio (Xiamen) Biotechnology Co., Ltd. It consists of a light source system, a photoelectric detection system, a signal amplifier circuit, a thermal printer, and a display screen.

IgM anti-A and anti-B detection using the PFA
To achieve rapid blood type antibody detection, the following steps are performed. First, 60 μL of plasma is directly added to the sample reaction well without dilution for blood type detection. For antibody titer detection, 10 μL of plasma is mixed with 70 μL of saline to achieve a dilution factor of 8. The subsequent steps are identical for both types of detection. The sample is gently mixed by the operator for 5 min to ensure uniformity. The reaction zone of the detection card is then inverted to allow the liquid to flow into the filtration zone, and 150 μL of saline is added to rinse the free RBCbm@Fluo. Finally, fluorescence intensity is measured using a portable fluorescence analyzer to determine both the blood type and antibody titer.

IgM anti-A and anti-B agglutination titers using GMA
All procedures were carried out according to the manufacturer’s instructions. A 50 μL aliquot of serially diluted serum and 50 μL of a 0.8% RBC suspension of either group A or B were added to the gel card microcolumns (ABO reverse typing card, Bioxun). The card was then centrifuged, and the titer was defined as the highest dilution showing 1+ agglutination.

Clinical evaluation
The study was preregistered in the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2300078864; first posted on 20 December 2023, http://www.chictr.org). The clinical evaluation started on 23 April 2024 and was conducted by trained healthcare professionals from the participating clinical institutions and our research team in accordance with institutional guidelines. Routine residual blood samples from adult patients (18–65 years) were eligible, including anticoagulated venous whole blood and/or serum/plasma, collected within 48 h and stored at 2–8 °C prior to testing. Samples were excluded if obtained from infants <4 months or patients >65 years, or if they showed severe hemolysis, lipemia, turbidity, contamination, or originated from patients with severe conditions that may affect blood group antibody detection (e.g., cancer, leukemia, multiple myeloma, Parkinson’s disease, liver disease, tuberculosis). Peripheral blood (~5 mL) was processed by centrifugation at 3000×g for 5 min to separate plasma from RBCs and buffy coat; plasma/serum was used for antibody-related analyses. Each sample was assigned a unique identifier and tested in random order under double-blind conditions. The primary outcomes were sensitivity, specificity, and overall concordance between the POCT method and the standard microcolumn gel card method; secondary outcomes included the kappa coefficient and related agreement statistics. The outcomes reported in the study protocol/registry and in this manuscript are consistent. The preregistered target recruitment was 3000 blood samples and 488 antibody titer samples; however, due to a phased clinical trial design, we enrolled 641 blood samples and 388 antibody titer samples across two phases. This sample-size deviation reflects the phased implementation and availability of eligible residual samples during the study period; hospital approval was obtained to use the corresponding routine clinical results. No other protocol deviations or analysis-plan changes were made.

Statistics and reproducibility
Statistical analysis was conducted using GraphPad Prism version 9.2 (GraphPad Software Inc.) and Medcalc version 23.1.7 (Medcalc Software Inc.). A P value <0.05 was considered statistically significant for all tests. Data are presented as mean values ± standard deviation. Statistical comparisons between groups are described in the figure legends. Each experiment included at least three data sets. Linear regression analysis was used for parameter optimization. Pearson’s correlation test was employed for data analysis. The Pearson correlation coefficient (r) measures the strength of the linear relationship between two variables, where a value of |r|>0.8 indicates a strong correlation. Linear regression and Pearson’s correlation were used to analyze the IgM anti-A and anti-B titers between the two techniques.

The following concordance rates were calculated:

Positive Concordance Rate (Sensitivity) = (True Positive (A) / (True Positive (A) + False Negative (C))) × 100%

Negative Concordance Rate (Specificity) = (True Negative (D) / (False Positive (B) + True Negative (D))) × 100%

Overall Concordance Rate = ((A + D) / (A + B + C + D)) × 100%

The cutoff value was determined based on the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve and the optimal Youden index. Cohen’s Kappa (κ) was used to assess the agreement between the two methods.

No statistical method was used to predetermine sample size for laboratory experiments. For the clinical trial, sample size was calculated as follows. To meet the requirements of the study, we first designed the experiment with the following criteria: antibody titers were categorized into six groups (≤1:16, 1:32, 1:64, 1:128, 1:256, ≥1:512), with each group containing at least 30 samples. Using a significance level of 0.05 and a statistical power of 80%, the estimated total sample size required for the experiment was calculated to be between 168 and 180. Therefore, at least 360 clinical samples with unknown blood types were tested to meet the study’s requirements. No data were excluded from the analyses. The clinical trial was conducted under a double-blind design. The experiments in Figs. 2b, c, i, 3d, e, 4e, h, 5g and Supplementary Figs. 5, 6, 14 were independently repeated three times with similar results.

1. In general, the section related to membrane integrity should be reinforced. Although the results provide strong validation of
the system, this aspect would benefit from being revised or presented in a different manner by the authors.
• In line 272, the sentence “TEM results for RBCbm@Fluo (Fig. 1a) confirmed the integrity of the cell membrane” is not
entirely accurate. The TEM images provided are not sufficient to support such a statement, and it is recommended that this
phrase be removed.
• Line 285: Figure 2f shows significant differences between membranes, and in both the bm and bm-Fluo conditions, a well-
defined membrane is not observed as it is in the other samples. Similarly, in the confocal images (Fig. 2g), actin appears
disrupted.
• Line 331: This statement contradicts earlier claims that the membrane remains intact.
2. Although the paper reports 100% accuracy for ABO blood typing (which is excellent), the 80.75% concordance with the
reference method for antibody titration is a point that requires further analysis and justification.
Is this level of concordance acceptable in clinical practice for all antibody titration applications (e.g., in monitoring

Are these due to inherent methodological differences, variability in the reference methods, or limitations of the PFA in certain

Comparing this performance with the known intra- and inter-laboratory variability of traditional methods would also

3. The paper predominantly focuses on the detection of IgM anti-A and anti-B antibodies. Although it mentions the potential

Is the method equally effective for detecting IgG antibodies? If not, what are the challenges in adapting the system for IgG

Is the bioengineering process for RBCs easily scalable to meet mass demand? Are there significant regulatory or cost-

variants can vary significantly across populations.
Was the method tested on samples from individuals of different ethnic backgrounds or with less common antigenic variants?
6. Overall, it is recommended that the manuscript be reviewed carefully to correct grammatical errors, spacing issues, and
